engagement.coverage_declaration: What was exercised. The runtime attack surface was the priority, because this library is placed in front of inbound HTTP requests by its own middlewares (openapi3filter/middleware.go, openapi3filter/validation_handler.go): openapi3filter (parameter and body decoding for path, query, header, cookie and every registered body decoder; request and response validation; the security-requirement pass), both routers, the openapi3 loader and $ref resolution, and the JSON Schema validation engine (schema.go visit* path, schema_pattern.go, schema_formats.go) together with the document model needed to follow them (paths.go, path_item.go, maplike.go, origin.go). Pack sections consulted, and only after the unaided reading was written down: web-api.md §0, §5; web-api-clientside-logic.md §8, §9 (WEB-23, WEB-26); local-app.md §5 (LOC-10); infra-cloud-cicd-exposure.md §4 (INF-15, INF-16); supply-chain.md §5 (SUP-09); supply-chain-secrets-malware.md §8 (secret formats). What was NOT exercised, and where silence is silence rather than a clean bill: openapi2, openapi2conv and openapi3conv (the Swagger 2.0 model and the conversions), openapi3gen, openapi3/internalize_refs.go, openapi3/walk.go and openapi3/validation_error.go, and the README and generated .github/docs/*.txt. The ~5,000 files under openapi2/testdata and openapi3/testdata were scanned for high-precision secret formats only (see ruled_out) and were not read as documents. Standard families actually exercised: CWE, OWASP Top 10 2025, ASVS 5.0 V5/V8/V11, CICD-SEC and SLSA Build. Not exercised: WSTG (no live target), MASVS/MASTG (no mobile artifact), the LLM and agentic families (no LLM call anywhere in the module), NIST 800-53 beyond the SC references carried by the procedures. Bound on depth: no Go toolchain exists on this host, so nothing was compiled, executed, fuzzed or tested - every finding rests on reading the code, and every `verification` field says `not executed` for that reason. No remote target was contacted and no dependency source was available (github.com/oasdiff/yaml3, github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6 and github.com/gorilla/mux were reasoned about from their call sites only, which is why F-013 is `probable` rather than settled). No dependency was checked against any advisory database, by instruction; the supply-chain reading here is about provenance and pinning, not about known CVEs in the eleven modules of go.mod.

dropped.label: circular-ref-recursion-in-loader
dropped.reason: A circular $ref does not recurse without bound: shouldVisitRef refuses a ref already present in loader.visitedRefs and registers a backtrack callback instead of descending, and visitRef/unvisitRef maintain that set around every descent. The `visited []string` parameter threaded through resolveSchemaRef is dead - never appended to, never read - which is what made this look unguarded, but it is not the mechanism that protects the walk.

dropped.label: regexp-compiled-per-query-key-in-deepobject-loop
dropped.reason: The deepObject branch compiles two regular expressions inside the per-query-key loop, which is wasteful, but the parameter name is passed through regexp.QuoteMeta so no pattern is attacker-authored and the cost is linear in the number of query keys. The only reason to keep it is as part of the same deepObject decoding path, where the real resource issue lives.

findings.title: Unauthenticated remote panic: PathItem.GetOperation panics on any non-standard HTTP method, and the legacy router hands it req.Method verbatim
findings.evidence: openapi3/path_item.go:153-175 GetOperation switches on the nine net/http method constants and its default branch is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`. routers/legacy/router.go:105 takes `method, url := req.Method, req.URL` and never normalises or allow-lists it. At line 137 `root.Match(method + " " + remainingPath)` fails for any method the spec did not register (the pattern tree holds only the uppercase methods returned by PathItem.Operations()), so `route == nil`. Line 148 then looks the path up verbatim: `pathItem := doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath)`, a plain map lookup (openapi3/maplike.go:275-282) that returns non-nil for any static path key such as "/pets". Line 150 calls `pathItem.GetOperation(method)` with the attacker's method -> default branch -> panic. openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:39 builds exactly this router (`legacyrouter.NewRouter(doc)`) and openapi3filter/validation_handler.go:84 calls FindRoute on every inbound request, before ValidateRequest and therefore before any authentication.
findings.impact: Any remote client aborts request processing at will with one request - `curl -X BREW https://host/pets`, or a lowercase `-X get` - against any path that appears literally in the spec. Under net/http the panic hits the per-connection recover, so the effect is a dropped connection plus a full stack trace in the server log for every such request: a cheap unauthenticated connection-reset and log-flooding primitive. In any caller that validates outside a recovered net/http handler (a worker goroutine, a queue or gRPC adapter, a framework with no recovery middleware) the same request kills the process.
findings.preconditions: The application uses routers/legacy - directly, or through openapi3filter.ValidationHandler, which selects it unconditionally - and the document contains at least one path key with no template variable, so that Paths.Value(remainingPath) hits. If the document declares servers, the request must match one (routers/legacy/router.go:118-122 returns ErrPathNotFound otherwise), which any request the deployment already serves does by construction: the method is the only thing the attacker changes. No credentials are needed.
findings.recommendation: Do not panic on data that arrives from the network. Give PathItem a non-panicking lookup that returns nil for an unknown method and use it at routers/legacy/router.go:150; or reject any method outside the known set in FindRoute before the lookup and return routers.ErrMethodNotAllowed. Keep the panicking variant only for the programmatic SetOperation path, where the argument is the caller's own constant.
findings.limits: That net/http delivers an arbitrary RFC 9110 token as req.Method without rewriting it is a property of the Go standard library, not of this repository, and is not re-derived here. No Go toolchain exists on the audit host, so the panic was established by reading the switch and its default branch rather than by executing it. routers/gorillamux was checked and is not affected: its mux route is built with .Methods(<uppercase spec methods>), so a non-standard method never matches and router.go:116 is never reached with one.

findings.title: An array index taken from the query string sizes a slice: one request allocates gigabytes in openapi3filter deepObject decoding
findings.evidence: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:638) turns `?p[arr][N]=x` into props["arr\x1FN"]: lines 669-679 make every `[...]` group of the query key a path segment. makeObject (line 911) splits on that delimiter and deepSet builds mobj = {"arr": {"N": "x"}}. buildResObj (line 965) reaches the `array` branch at line 972 and calls sliceMapToSlice(t) at line 982. sliceMapToSlice (line 936) parses the key with `strconv.Atoi` at line 941 with no upper bound, takes `max` over the keys at lines 947-952, then runs `for i := 0; i <= max; i++ { result = append(result, ...) }` at line 953. N is the attacker's decimal literal, so `?p[arr][2000000000]=x` grows `result` to 2e9 interface headers (~32 GB) before any schema rule - maxItems, maxLength, type - is consulted. Line 986 then allocates a second slice of the same length. Nothing between the query string and line 953 compares the index against a value the client does not control.
findings.impact: Unauthenticated memory exhaustion. One short GET request drives the process into the OOM killer, or into a multi-second allocation and GC storm, taking the whole service down; it is trivially repeatable and needs no session.
findings.preconditions: The spec declares a query parameter with `style: deepObject` whose schema is an object with an array-typed property (or an array-typed additionalProperties schema). openapi3filter must be in the request path, which is its purpose. Security requirements, if the operation has any, are checked first (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:52), so on a secured operation a valid credential is needed; on any operation without security requirements it is reachable anonymously.
findings.recommendation: Bound the index before it sizes anything: in sliceMapToSlice reject an index above a configured maximum and above the number of values actually supplied, and build the result from the sorted keys present rather than from `0..max`. Absent positions are already filled with nil, so driving the loop from len(m) loses nothing.
findings.limits: Establishes memory exhaustion, not code execution or data disclosure. The per-element byte cost was not measured on a running process (no Go toolchain on the audit host); the unbounded growth itself is read directly from the loop bound at line 953.

findings.title: Unchecked type assertion in deepSet: two colliding deepObject query keys panic the request
findings.evidence: deepSet (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:899) walks intermediate keys with `m = m[key].(map[string]any)` at line 905, with no comma-ok. makeObject (line 914) feeds it every entry of the props map in Go's randomised map order. The query string `?p[a]=1&p[a][b]=2` produces, through the deepObject branch at lines 661-687, props = {"a": "1", "a\x1Fb": "2"}. If the shorter key is applied first, mobj["a"] holds the string "1"; the longer key then asserts that string to map[string]any and panics with `interface conversion: interface {} is string, not map[string]interface {}`. Which key comes first is not stable, so the panic fires on roughly half of identical requests.
findings.impact: A remote client aborts request processing at will and, in the common net/http deployment, forces a stack trace into the log and a connection reset on every attempt; outside a recovered handler the process dies. Unlike F-001 this needs no static path in the spec, only a deepObject object parameter.
findings.preconditions: The spec declares a query parameter with `style: deepObject` and an object schema. Reachable without credentials on any operation that carries no security requirement.
findings.recommendation: Use the comma-ok form in deepSet and return a ParseError when an intermediate key already holds a scalar - the same class of error makeObject already raises at lines 916-920 for implicit array indexes - so the conflict becomes a 400 rather than a panic. Sorting the props keys before the deepSet loop would also make the outcome deterministic.
findings.limits: The roughly even hit rate follows from Go's documented map-iteration randomisation and was not measured; the panic itself is unconditional once the shorter key is applied first. Not executed - no Go toolchain on the audit host.

findings.title: The legacy router collapses two spec paths that differ only by a trailing slash, so the operation used for validation is chosen at random
findings.evidence: CreateNode strips every trailing slash from the pattern before building the tree (routers/legacy/pathpattern/node.go:164-166) and Match strips them again from the request path (lines 253-255). routers/legacy/router.go:66-77 iterates `doc.Paths.Map()` - a Go map, so in randomised order - calling root.Add(method+" "+path, route) for each entry. "/pets" and "/pets/" therefore resolve to the same node, and Add sets `node.Value = value` (node.go:158), so the second registration silently replaces the first. Nothing in openapi3 rejects a document declaring both: Paths.Validate (openapi3/paths.go:41-75) only refuses two paths whose templated normalisation collides, and "/pets" and "/pets/" do not. Requests to either spelling then validate against whichever of the two operations happened to be registered last in that process.
findings.impact: The request is validated against the wrong operation: its parameters, its request-body schema and - through openapi3filter/validate_request.go:46-51 - its security requirements. If the two path items differ in security, a client reaching the protected spelling can be validated under the unprotected operation, and the outcome flips between process restarts, which makes it hard to reproduce or attribute.
findings.preconditions: The document declares two path keys differing only by trailing slashes, with different operations, and the application uses routers/legacy - the router openapi3filter.ValidationHandler selects.
findings.recommendation: Detect the collision instead of overwriting silently: have pathpattern.Node.Add refuse to overwrite a node that already carries a value and surface that as an error from legacy.NewRouter; or normalise trailing slashes in openapi3.Paths.Validate so the pair is reported as conflicting paths at load time.
findings.limits: The collapse and the last-writer-wins overwrite are read directly from the code. Whether any real document declares such a pair, and therefore whether the security-requirement swap is exercised anywhere, is not established here. The same EqualSuffix comparison (node.go:114-116) also treats "{a}" and "{b}" as one suffix, but that pair is already rejected by Paths.Validate as conflicting paths.

findings.title: legacy FindRoute can return a nil route together with a nil error, and dereferences a nil node on the same fall-through
findings.evidence: routers/legacy/router.go:145-162: when `route == nil` the function checks `doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath)` and `pathItem.GetOperation(method)`, and if both are non-nil it does not return - it falls through to `paramKeys := node.VariableNames` (line 158) and then `return route, pathParams, nil` (line 162) with route still nil. Two defects share that fall-through. (a) `node` is nil whenever Match failed, so line 158 is a nil-pointer dereference. (b) When Match succeeded but node.Value is not a *routers.Route, the caller receives (nil, params, nil), and every caller reads a nil error as success - openapi3filter/validate_request.go:40-41 immediately does `route.Operation`. Case (b) is concretely reachable through Router.AddRoute (lines 82-93), which stores `router` (a *Router) as the node value while FindRoute at line 139 asserts `node.Value.(*routers.Route)`; that assertion can never succeed for an AddRoute-registered path.
findings.impact: A nil-pointer panic in the request path - the same availability effect as F-001 and F-003 - plus a contract violation, a nil route with a nil error, that moves the panic into the caller's code where it is harder to diagnose.
findings.preconditions: For (b): the application registers routes through Router.AddRoute rather than only through NewRouter, and the request path is also a key in doc.Paths with the requested method defined. For (a): a router/document state in which Match yields nothing while Paths.Value and GetOperation both succeed.
findings.recommendation: Return an explicit error instead of falling through: if route is still nil after the Paths.Value/GetOperation checks, return routers.ErrPathNotFound or a dedicated error; guard line 158 with `if node != nil`; and make AddRoute store a *routers.Route so the assertion at line 139 can succeed.
findings.inference: That a consumer calls Router.AddRoute, or otherwise reaches a state where Match fails while the path and method exist in the document. The mismatch between what AddRoute stores and what FindRoute asserts is read directly from the code, but no call site inside this repository exercises it.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A test that builds a legacy Router with NewRouter, adds a route with AddRoute for a static path already present in the document, and calls FindRoute on that path: it should show either the nil-route/nil-error return or the nil dereference at routers/legacy/router.go:158.

triage.reason: Router.AddRoute is exported and shipped (routers/legacy/router.go:82) but has no call site inside this repository, so whether a real consumer exercises the path cannot be established from the tree.

findings.limits: Does not establish that any published consumer calls AddRoute. Branch (a) is a code-shape defect whose trigger could not be constructed from a plain document within this reading.

findings.title: A schema pattern that fails to compile leaves a nil matcher, and under MultiError the next line calls MatchString on it
findings.evidence: openapi3/schema.go:2654-2666: `cpiface, _ := compiledPatterns.Load(schema.Pattern)`, `cp, _ := cpiface.(RegexMatcher)`, and if cp is nil, `if cp, err = schema.compilePattern(settings.regexCompiler); err != nil { if !settings.multiError { return err }; me = append(me, err) }`. openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-31 shows compilePattern returning the zero matcher together with the error - on the default path `cp, err = regexp.Compile(intoGoRegexp(pattern))`, so cp holds a nil *regexp.Regexp. Execution then falls straight into `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at line 2666, calling MatchString on a nil receiver (or on a nil interface, if a custom RegexCompilerFunc returned one) - a nil-pointer dereference. The guard exists only on the `!settings.multiError` branch. openapi3filter/validate_request.go:236-238 and 340-342 set exactly that flag whenever the caller passes Options{MultiError: true}, for both parameters and request bodies.
findings.impact: Every request whose validation reaches that string field panics: connection reset plus a stack trace under net/http, process death in a caller without recovery. Which schema branch is visited is chosen by the request body or parameter, so a client can steer validation into the branch carrying the uncompilable pattern.
findings.preconditions: openapi3filter Options.MultiError (or openapi3.MultiErrors()) enabled, and a `pattern` that fails to compile at request time. Two ways that happens: the document was never validated with pattern checking - routers/gorillamux does not validate at all and openapi3.DisableSchemaPatternValidation exists for exactly this case, as does cmd/validate's --patterns flag ('allows schema patterns unsupported by the Go regexp engine') - or a custom Options.RegexCompiler rejects a pattern the default engine accepted.
findings.recommendation: Return the error (or skip the pattern check) when compilePattern fails, instead of falling through: `if err != nil { ...; me = append(me, err) }` must be followed by a guard on cp before line 2666. Also make compilePattern return an explicit nil matcher on error so a caller cannot accidentally use a typed-nil regexp.
findings.inference: Reachability: no configuration in this repository both enables MultiError and carries an uncompilable pattern, so the combination is inferred from the exported options that make it expressible rather than observed in a running deployment.
findings.what_would_settle_it: A unit test calling Schema{Pattern: "^(?=x)"}.VisitJSON("x", openapi3.MultiErrors()) - a lookahead is valid ECMA-262 and rejected by Go's regexp - which should panic at openapi3/schema.go:2666 rather than return a MultiError.
findings.limits: No test in the repository exercises MultiErrors together with an uncompilable pattern (checked openapi3/schema_pattern_test.go and every EnableMultiError/MultiErrors use in openapi3), so the branch is untested rather than proven harmless. Not executed - no Go toolchain on the audit host.

findings.title: Request bodies are buffered whole, twice, before the checks that would reject them, with no size limit anywhere in the library
findings.evidence: openapi3filter/validate_request.go:271 `data, err = io.ReadAll(req.Body)` reads the entire body with no bound, and only afterwards does the function check whether the operation declares any content at all (line 303 `if len(content) == 0 { return nil }`) or whether the request's Content-Type is one the spec accepts (lines 308-316). validateSecurityRequirement does the same at line 448, before the AuthenticationFunc is ever called (line 492), so a request that authentication will reject has already been buffered. `grep -rn 'MaxBytesReader' --include='*.go'` over the whole repository returns nothing, and the only ContentLength uses are assignments made after the body has been read (lines 287, 384, 484, 513). The body decoders reinforce this: PlainBodyDecoder, FileBodyDecoder and UrlencodedBodyDecoder each call io.ReadAll again (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1348, 1651, 1400).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client makes the server commit memory proportional to what it chooses to send, on requests that are guaranteed to be rejected - a wrong Content-Type, a bad credential. The cost is paid twice per request (the security pass and the body pass) plus once more inside the decoder, and it is paid before any validation decision.
findings.preconditions: The deploying application does not wrap the body itself; Go's net/http applies no default limit. Reachable on any operation, and on any operation with no security requirement it needs no credential.
findings.recommendation: Cap the read: use io.LimitReader / http.MaxBytesReader with a configurable maximum in Options, and check Content-Type and the presence of declared content before reading the body rather than after. Read once and share the buffer between the security pass and the body pass instead of reading twice.
findings.inference: Whether a limit exists is a property of the deploying application (an ingress limit, a http.MaxBytesReader in the caller's own middleware), which is outside this repository; the absence of any bound inside the library is observed, the absence of one in front of it is not.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The deployment's ingress/proxy body-size configuration, or the consumer's middleware chain, showing whether anything wraps req.Body before openapi3filter sees it.

triage.reason: A caller-side or ingress body limit would bound this, and no such artifact was provided; per FP-08 the same reasoning applies to any control outside the repository, so this cannot be answered HOLDS.

findings.limits: Names the missing bound inside the library; it does not establish that any particular deployment lacks one in front. The double read and the read-before-check ordering hold regardless of an external limit.

findings.title: CI job exports GITHUB_TOKEN to every step, including steps that run unpinned third-party code, and declares no permissions block
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/go.yml:7-12 sets `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` at job level, so it is in the environment of every step. Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml declares a `permissions:` key, so the token carries the repository/organisation default scope. Steps that inherit it include `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -fix ./...` (line 68), `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest ./...` (line 108), `go run -a github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/cmd/validate@latest` (line 137) and, in the check-goimports job, `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` - each of which downloads and executes code resolved at run time. Both workflows trigger on `push` and `pull_request`.
findings.impact: Any of those `@latest` modules, if compromised upstream, executes inside the job with the job's GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment. If the repository default is read-write, that is write access to repository contents from a build step; even read-only it is a credential handed to third-party code that has no need of it.
findings.preconditions: On `push` the job runs with the repository's own token. Fork pull_request runs receive a read-only token, so the write case depends on the default workflow-permission setting, which lives outside the tree.
findings.recommendation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level and grant more only on the job that needs it; drop the job-level GITHUB_TOKEN export and pass the token only to the step that requires it, if any does. Replace `@latest` in `go run`/`go install` with versions pinned in a tools file so the executed code is the code the module graph already verifies with `go mod verify`.
findings.inference: The effective scope of GITHUB_TOKEN: with no permissions block it comes from the repository/organisation default workflow permission, which is not represented anywhere in the tree.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The repository's Settings -> Actions -> General -> Workflow permissions value, or an exported organisation ruleset, showing whether the default token is read-only or read-write.

triage.reason: The default GITHUB_TOKEN permission is a GitHub console setting; no exported artifact for it was provided, so per FP-08 it cannot be answered HOLDS.

findings.limits: No claim is made that any referenced module is malicious today; the finding is the standing exposure, not an incident.

findings.title: Every GitHub Action and every CI tool is referenced by a mutable pointer - a tag or @latest - and none by commit SHA
findings.evidence: None of the seven action references under .github/workflows/ is pinned by a 40-character SHA. go.yml uses actions/setup-go@v6 (line 27), actions/cache@v3 (line 32) and actions/checkout@v6 (line 44), and repeats setup-go/checkout in the check-goimports job; shellcheck.yml uses actions/checkout@v2 (line 12) and the third-party ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (line 14). The same holds for executable dependencies: `go run ...modernize@latest`, `go run ...nilness@latest` and `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` resolve at run time, a weaker pointer than a tag. actions/checkout@v2 is additionally several majors behind.
findings.impact: A tag is a movable pointer under the upstream owner's control: whoever holds that account, or an attacker who steals its credentials, changes what runs in this pipeline with no change in this repository. Combined with F-008 the code that arrives that way runs with the job's token in its environment.
findings.preconditions: Upstream compromise or a malicious retag; nothing in this repository has to change.
findings.recommendation: Pin every `uses:` to a full commit SHA with the human-readable version in a trailing comment, and let Dependabot or Renovate bump them. Replace the `@latest` tool invocations with versions pinned through the module graph.

triage.reason: No compromise is demonstrated in any referenced action or module today, so this is defence in depth against a supply-chain event rather than an exploit path; the reference counts are read from .github/workflows/go.yml and .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml.

findings.limits: Counts references under .github/workflows/ only; no integrity or reachability check was run against the upstream repositories.

findings.title: Loading external $refs has one all-or-nothing switch: no scheme, host or root-directory allowlist, no timeout, and a process-global cache that never evicts
findings.evidence: Once IsExternalRefsAllowed is true, openapi3/loader.go:107-112 is the only gate and it is boolean. ReadFromFile (openapi3/loader_uri_reader.go:79-84) then does `os.ReadFile(path.Clean(filepath.FromSlash(location.Path)))` with no containment to the document's directory, so `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` resolves; resolvePath (openapi3/loader.go:307-319) explicitly returns an absolute componentPath unchanged. ReadFromHTTP (lines 51-70) is built on http.DefaultClient, which has no timeout, applies no allowlist to the host, and finishes with an unbounded io.ReadAll (line 68) - `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/..."` is fetched as written. URIMapCache (lines 90-117) keeps every fetched document in a map captured by the package-level DefaultReadFromURI var, never evicted; its own comment says it suits short-lived processes, yet it is the default for every Loader, including a long-lived server.
findings.impact: A service that validates or renders documents supplied by its users, with external refs enabled (cmd/validate --ext is the shipped example), reads arbitrary local files and issues arbitrary outbound GETs on their behalf, hangs indefinitely on a slow host, and accumulates every fetched byte for the process lifetime.
findings.preconditions: IsExternalRefsAllowed set to true, or a custom ReadFromURIFunc installed - in which case the loader documents at openapi3/loader.go:39-49 that its own flag is not enforced at all and the custom function owns the policy.
findings.recommendation: Offer the policy the flag cannot express: an optional root directory that file refs must resolve inside (compare the cleaned absolute path against it before opening), an optional scheme/host allowlist for HTTP refs, an http.Client with a timeout as the default rather than http.DefaultClient, a response size cap on the ReadAll, and a cache with a bound or an opt-in constructor for long-lived processes.

triage.reason: Reading other files is the declared purpose of IsExternalRefsAllowed (openapi3/loader.go:29-31) and of cmd/validate's --ext flag (cmd/validate/main.go:26-28), and the ReadFromURIFunc field carries an explicit SECURITY note at openapi3/loader.go:39-49. Per FP-05 the finding therefore moves rather than disappearing: what is missing is any narrower policy than on/off, plus the timeout and cache bounds.

findings.limits: This is a library-default finding, not a demonstrated exploit against this repository: no consumer here enables external refs on untrusted input. cmd/validate reads a local file named on the command line, which is the operator's own choice.

findings.title: The compiled-pattern cache is process-global and keyed by the pattern string alone, so a configured RegexCompiler can be silently bypassed
findings.evidence: compilePattern stores its result with `compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)` (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:33) into the package-level `compiledPatterns sync.Map` declared at openapi3/schema.go:46, keyed only by the pattern text - not by which RegexCompilerFunc produced it. visitJSONString reads that cache first (openapi3/schema.go:2655-2657) and only calls compilePattern, with settings.regexCompiler, when the lookup misses. So the first compiler to see a given pattern anywhere in the process wins for every later validation of the same pattern text, whichever compiler that validation configured through Options.RegexCompiler or SetSchemaRegexCompiler. The map is also never evicted.
findings.impact: A caller that installs a stricter or differently-dialected regex engine for one document may still be matched by the default RE2 result cached from another - the override is not honoured and nothing reports that. In a process that loads many documents (a linting or gateway service), the map grows with every distinct pattern string and is never released.
findings.preconditions: Two validations in the same process with different RegexCompiler settings and an overlapping pattern string, or a long-lived process loading many documents.
findings.recommendation: Key the cache by the pair (compiler identity, pattern), or hold the compiled matcher on the Schema/settings rather than in a package-global; bound the map or make caching opt-in.

triage.reason: Go's RE2 engine has no catastrophic-backtracking behaviour to bypass, so no exploit path is claimed against the default configuration; the impact is a silently ignored caller override and unbounded cache growth, which is why this is filed as hardening.

findings.limits: Does not establish that any consumer installs a custom RegexCompiler for a security purpose. The pattern set is bounded by the documents loaded, so the growth matters only for a process that loads documents it does not control.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder decompresses without a bound and appends the whole scratch buffer regardless of how many bytes were read
findings.evidence: openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1614-1650: the whole body is copied into memory (io.Copy into a bytes.Buffer), `content := make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))` pre-sizes from the attacker-supplied entry count, and the read loop grows `content` with no cap on total decompressed size - the function's own doc comment says it 'may be susceptible to a zip bomb attack'. Separately, line 1637 is `content = append(content, buffer...)` inside `if 0 < n`, appending all 256 bytes of the scratch buffer instead of `buffer[:n]`, so every short read injects stale bytes from the previous iteration into the decoded value.
findings.impact: A consumer that registers this decoder accepts a decompression bomb on that content type. The append defect additionally corrupts the value that is then validated and handed to the application: the decoded text does not match the archive contents, so validation is performed against data the client did not send.
findings.preconditions: The decoder is not registered by default (see the init() list at openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1330-1345); a consumer must call RegisterBodyDecoder with it.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each entry's reader in an io.LimitReader with a total budget across entries, refuse an archive whose declared uncompressed size exceeds it, and fix line 1637 to `append(content, buffer[:n]...)`.

triage.reason: The decoder is opt-in and its doc comment at openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:1611-1612 names the zip-bomb risk, so the exposure is intended; per FP-05 the finding moves to what the comment does not cover - the append defect at line 1637, which is a correctness bug and is not documented anywhere.

findings.limits: Not registered by default, so no shipped configuration reaches it; the impact depends entirely on a consumer opting in.

findings.title: An element count read from the document sizes a slice in origin decoding, under Loader.IncludeOrigin
findings.evidence: openapi3/origin.go:99 `locs := make([]Location, count)` where `count := toInt(s[idx])` (line 97) is an element of the `__origin__` sequence being decoded, and the subsequent fill loop is separately bounded by `idx+2 < len(s)` (line 100) - so the allocation is sized by the declared count while the data that justifies it is not required to be present. Location is two strings plus four ints, so the multiplier is large. The `nf` branch above it (lines 65-66) does bound itself with `idx+nf*3 <= len(s)` before allocating, which is the shape the sequence branch is missing.
findings.impact: If the declared count can be attacker-influenced, a small document sizes a very large slice - the classic length-from-the-wire allocation. The path is off by default (openapi3/loader.go:21 IncludeOrigin = false) and only a service that loads documents it does not control while asking for origin tracking would be exposed.
findings.preconditions: Loader.IncludeOrigin (or the deprecated package global) set to true, and a document supplied by an untrusted party.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same bound the fields branch already uses: refuse to allocate more than the remaining elements of the sequence can fill, i.e. size from `min(count, (len(s)-idx)/3)`, and grow by append rather than pre-sizing.
findings.inference: Whether the `__origin__` value that reaches originFromSeq can be the document's own text at all: the sequence is described as 'produced by yaml3's addOrigin' (openapi3/origin.go:40), and whether that library overwrites, merges with, or defers to a `__origin__` key already present in the source document cannot be read from this tree - github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 is not vendored and no Go module cache exists on the audit host.
findings.what_would_settle_it: The addOrigin implementation in github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 (does it inject its own `__origin__` unconditionally, or can a document-supplied one survive?), or a test that loads a document containing a literal `__origin__` sequence with a huge count under Loader{IncludeOrigin: true}.

triage.reason: Whether `count` traces back to the document text or only to library-generated structure depends on github.com/oasdiff/yaml3, which is not present in the tree or in any module cache on this host.

findings.limits: The missing bound at line 99 is observed; attacker control of the value is not. Reported at low severity precisely because the source of `count` could not be settled inside the scope.

findings.title: An OpenAPI 3.1 array parameter without `items` passes document validation and then nil-dereferences on the first request that supplies it
findings.evidence: openapi3/schema.go:1689-1692 requires `items` for an array only when `!validationOpts.jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled` and there is no `prefixItems`; openapi3/openapi3.go:268-274 makes T.Validate append IsOpenAPI31OrLater() for any 3.1/3.2 document, and openapi3/validation_options.go:38-44 shows that option setting jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled = true. So `type: array` with no `items` is accepted for every 3.1 document - correctly, since it is legal JSON Schema 2020-12. The decoders then dereference that nil unconditionally. Query: decodeValue (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:323-330) routes an array schema to DecodeArray, which calls d.parseArray at line 544, which at line 555 does `d.parseValue(v, schemaRef.Value.Items)` with a nil *SchemaRef; parseValue starts at line 580 with `len(schema.Value.AllOf)` - a nil dereference. Header, cookie and path parameters reach the package-level parseArray at line 1103, whose line 1106 calls `parsePrimitive(v, schemaRef.Value.Items)`, and parsePrimitive starts at line 1128 with `schema.Value.Type.Slice()` - the same dereference. A urlencoded body has its own copy at line 1398, `items := propSchema.Value.Items.Value`, reached before any request data is even parsed. Nothing on any of these three paths tests Items for nil, and none of them consults prefixItems either, so `prefixItems` without `items` fails identically.
findings.impact: Every request that supplies the parameter panics: connection reset plus a stack trace under net/http, process death in a caller without recovery. The document is not malformed - it passed the library's own Validate - so the defect only appears in production, on the first client that sends the field.
findings.preconditions: An OpenAPI 3.1 (or 3.2) document with an array-typed parameter, or an array-typed property of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, that omits `items`. The attacker only has to send the parameter; no credentials are needed on an operation without security requirements.
findings.recommendation: Treat a missing `items` as 'no constraint on elements' rather than as a guaranteed pointer: in parseValue, parsePrimitive and UrlencodedBodyDecoder, return the raw string unvalidated when the item schema is nil, and consult prefixItems where it applies. A defensive nil check at each of the three call sites (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:555, 1106, 1398) is the minimum.
findings.limits: Applies to 3.1+ documents only: for a 3.0 document openapi3/schema.go:1690 rejects the shape at load time, which is the compensating control that does not carry over. The request-body path is unaffected - visitJSONArray guards `if itemSchemaRef := schema.Items; itemSchemaRef != nil` at openapi3/schema.go:2797 - so this is a parameter- and urlencoded-decoder defect, not a schema-validation one. Not executed: no Go toolchain on the audit host.

ruled_out.class: Tracked secrets in the working tree
ruled_out.where: Whole tree except .git, scanned for the distinctive credential formats (GitHub personal-access-token prefix, AWS access-key-ID prefix, Anthropic key prefix, Slack token prefixes, PEM private-key headers) and for `password|secret|token|api_key` assignments in non-test Go sources. One hit, in a test fixture, dropped for the reason recorded in unaided_pass.dropped. Git history was NOT scanned: reading it was excluded by the engagement instruction, so SUP-17 is unexercised, not clean.

ruled_out.class: Unbounded recursion / stack exhaustion through circular $ref
ruled_out.where: openapi3/loader.go resolveSchemaRef and the visitRef/shouldVisitRef/unvisitRef trio (lines 366-392). Bounded to schema refs reached from ResolveRefsIn within a single document; the equivalent walks in internalize_refs.go and walk.go were not read.

No database/sql, no os/exec and no html/template anywhere in the module; the single text/template use is openapi3/refsgenerator.go, which carries `//go:build ignore` and is therefore not compiled into any package. Bound: source grep across all non-test .go files.

ruled_out.class: Non-standard HTTP method reaching PathItem.GetOperation through the gorillamux router
ruled_out.where: routers/gorillamux/router.go:69 registers each route with .Methods(<uppercase methods from pathItem.Operations()>), so mux cannot match a request whose method is outside that set and line 116 is never reached with an unknown method; the mismatch surfaces as routers.ErrMethodNotAllowed at line 121. This is the control the legacy router lacks (F-001).

ruled_out.class: patternProperties and other 2020-12 keywords silently unenforced at request time
ruled_out.where: For pre-3.1 documents openapi3/schema.go:1464-1467 rejects patternProperties at document-validation time; for 3.1 documents openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242 and :354 and openapi3filter/validate_response.go:76 all add EnableJSONSchema2020(), which routes validation through the santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema compiler that implements those keywords. Bound: the three openapi3filter entry points; a caller invoking Schema.VisitJSON directly without that option still gets the legacy visitor.
